newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grains-Prompt cargo S.American beans sold.
newsitem.headline: China Grains-Prompt cargo S.American beans sold.

text.p: A panamax cargo of South American soybeans was heard sold very recently to China for prompt delivery to a middle China port, helping pressure futures, grains traders said on Thursday.
The cargo was sold at about US$316 per tonne, C&F China, a senior grains trader said.
The latest news of a sale followed on a slew of cargoes arriving at regular intervals at Chinese ports, pressuring futures, grains traders said.
"Chinese (soybean) futures have been declining in the last few days -- this (cargo) could well be contributing," said one trader.
On Thursday, July soybean futures in Shanghai had dropped to 3,260 yuan per tonne, compared to Tuesday's July close of 3,290 per tonne (US$396.60)
Shanghai soybean futures fell on Tuesday, with the most actively traded November contract closing at an intra-day low of 3,290 yuan per tonne, down six yuan from Monday's close.
Big short positions continued to depress the November and January 1998 contracts in Shanghai and enlarged volumes indicated more short positions had been built, a China trader said earlier.
The cash price of soybean and soymeal in China remained steady at about 3,000 yuan and 2,850 yuan per tonne respectively, traders said.
"Many people expected the (domestic soybean and meal cash) market to go up from May onwards, but until now it still hasn't happened," said one grains source.
Dalian soybean futures also had dropped, with July down to around 3,100 yuan per tonne compared to 3,200 yuan about three weeks ago, a source said.
"August soybean is below 3,100 and new crop soybean is at 2,900 yuan per tonne," he said.
According to a senior Chinese grain trader's estimates, at least another 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes of soybeans had been contracted.
"China has bought at least a total of 1.5 million tonnes of soybeans," he said, noting the amount was similar for soymeal.
"I think the supply is plentiful, both from imported cargoes and domestic availability," he said.
A Beijing-based feed mill source said summer demand for eggs and poultry was softer.
"Demand will pick up after October and November," the source said.
China's soybean imports in the first quarter of this year totalled 973,000 tonnes, close to the total imports for all of 1996, the China Securities newspaper said last month.
China's first quarter soybean meal imports totalled 1.073 million tonnes, a 483.1 percent increase over the same period in 1996, the report said.
The source at the major feed mill said that if soybean meal prices went up, the mill would simply change its feed formula to add a bigger proportion of fish meal and reduce the proportion of soymeal.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
